newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Britain's Gurkhas--empire warriors, now HK doormen.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Gurkhas--empire warriors, now HK doormen.

text.p: Gurkhas once willing to fight and die defending Britain's empire now stand guard just inside the doors of Hong Kong's imposing banks and swish boutiques.
Their role over as front-line mercenaries recruited from the Himalayan kingdom of Nepal, they now protect a capitalist empire, impassive in dark trousers, blue shirts and berets.
As private security guards, mind-numbing routine -- not danger -- is their constant companion. No longer does the harsh battlefield atmosphere assault their senses.
Instead these stocky, tough warriors are stranded at duty posts amid air conditioning, the bleat of cell phones, and the scent of expensive perfumes trailed by elegant women shoppers.

"I know I'm fortunate to have this job and I'm better off than many Nepalese so I shouldn't complain," said a middle-aged ex-Gurkha working as a security guard at an upscale clothier in a Hong Kong shopping mall. Reluctant to speak at all, he refused to give his name.

"The problem is that I am bored and ashamed to be working as a store guard. Nothing happens. Life in the British army suited (me). I liked the work, I liked the travel. Now I am not making a very good living. I feel like my life is over but I don't blame anyone."
The Gurkhas battled their way into British hearts and history books with their bravery in countless military engagements since first being recruited in 1816.

They take pride in their reputation as front-line soldiers who never faltered when it came to close-quarter fighting, where they often employed their razor-sharp, curved kukri knives to devastating effect.
But a recent massive downscaling of British military forces and the looming handover of Hong Kong to China at midnight on June 30 have led to thousands of Gurkha redundancies.
Much-reduced, the Gurkha brigade once based in Hong Kong is now in Britain except under 200 Gurhas now on signals duty here.
Damar Thapa, 34, spent nine years as a British Gurkha before getting the axe as part of the army's redundancy scheme.

He counts himself lucky to have landed a job with Gurkha International Manpower Services, one of several security and employment firms created in Hong Kong to capitalise on the Gurkhas' reputation for courage, loyalty and integrity.
"The transition poses difficult feelings and challenges for everyone. I work in the employment office of this firm," Thapa said.

"The biggest problem so far is language because I dnn't speak Cantonese and that's what's needed (in the private sector) in Hong Kong. But if I were suddenly told to go work as a security guard in a mall I would face a big mental challenge. It would be difficult."
Another Hong Kong firm which seized upnn Gurkha redundancies as a business opportunity was Jardine Securicor Gurkha Services, which now employs 600 ex-servicemen in the security business.

"The Gurkhas are extremely well-travelled and well-trained men brought up in the culture of the British army," said Bill Thomas, general manager of Jardine's Gurkha operation. "All of our managers are former servicemen and police so we provide an organisation into which the Gurkha can fit comfortably."

Not every demobilised Gurkha has made it to Jardine. Some are employed as drivers and domestics. Others have returned to Nepal where their relatively meagre pensions go much further than in Hong Kong.
But Nepal is one of the world's poorer nations and one with a tradition of exporting primary wage earners, so there is family pressure on many Gurkhas to remain working in Hong Kong.
